entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18275"/><div sID="gen37971" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18275"/><hi type="bold">9. servants--</hi>"slaves."<div eID="gen37971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37972" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to please them well--</hi>"to give satisfaction" [Alford]. To be complaisant in everything; to have that zealous desire to gain the master's goodwill which will anticipate the master's wish and do even more than is required. The reason for the frequent recurrence of injunctions to slaves to subjection (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.5">Ep 6:5</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Col.3.22">Col 3:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.1">1Ti 6:1</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.18">1Pe 2:18</reference>) was, that in no rank was there more danger of the doctrine of the spiritual equality and freedom of Christians being misunderstood than in that of slaves. It was natural for the slave who had become a Christian, to forget his place and put himself on a social level with his master. Hence the charge for each to abide in the sphere in which he was when converted (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.20-1Cor.7.24">1Co 7:20-24</reference>).<div eID="gen37972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37973" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not answering again--</hi>in contradiction to the master: so the Greek, "not contradicting" [Wahl]. <div eID="gen37973" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 9. servants-- "slaves." to please them well-- "to give satisfaction" [Alford]. To be complaisant in everything; to have that zealous desire to gain the master's goodwill which will anticipate the master's wish and do even more than is required. The reason for the frequent recurrence of injunctions to slaves to subjection ( Ep 6:5 , &c.; Col 3:22 ; 1Ti 6:1 , &c.; 1Pe 2:18 ) was, that in no rank was there more danger of the doctrine of the spiritual equality and freedom of Christians being misunderstood than in that of slaves. It was natural for the slave who had become a Christian, to forget his place and put himself on a social level with his master. Hence the charge for each to abide in the sphere in which he was when converted ( 1Co 7:20-24 ). not answering again-- in contradiction to the master: so the Greek, "not contradicting" [Wahl].

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18276"/><div sID="gen37974" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18276"/><hi type="bold">10. Not purloining--</hi>Greek, "Not appropriating" what does not belong to one. It means "keeping back" dishonestly or deceitfully (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.2">Ac 5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.5.3">3</reference>).<div eID="gen37974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37975" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">showing--</hi>manifesting in acts.<div eID="gen37975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37976" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all--</hi>all possible.<div eID="gen37976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37977" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">good--</hi>really good; not so in mere appearance (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.5">Ep 6:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.22-Col.3.24">Col 3:22-24</reference>). "The heathen do not judge of the Christian's doctrines from the doctrine, but from his actions and life" [Chrysostom]. Men will write, fight, and even die for their religion; but how few live for it! Translate, "That they may adorn the doctrine of our Saviour God," that is, God the Father, the originating author of salvation (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.1">1Ti 1:1</reference>). God deigns to have His Gospel-doctrine adorned even by slaves, who are regarded by the world as no better than beasts of burden. "Though the service be rendered to an earthly master, the honor redounds to God, as the servant's goodwill flows from the fear of God" [Theophylact]. Even slaves, low as is their status, should not think the influence of their example a matter of no consequence to religion: how much more those in a high position. His love in being "our Saviour" is the strongest ground for our adorning His doctrine by our lives. This is the force of "For" in <reference osisRef="Titus.2.11">Tit 2:11</reference>. <div eID="gen37977" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 10. Not purloining-- Greek, "Not appropriating" what does not belong to one. It means "keeping back" dishonestly or deceitfully ( Ac 5:2 , 3 ). showing-- manifesting in acts. all-- all possible. good-- really good; not so in mere appearance ( Ep 6:5 , 6 ; Col 3:22-24 ). "The heathen do not judge of the Christian's doctrines from the doctrine, but from his actions and life" [Chrysostom]. Men will write, fight, and even die for their religion; but how few live for it! Translate, "That they may adorn the doctrine of our Saviour God," that is, God the Father, the originating author of salvation (compare Note, see on 1Ti 1:1 ). God deigns to have His Gospel-doctrine adorned even by slaves, who are regarded by the world as no better than beasts of burden. "Though the service be rendered to an earthly master, the honor redounds to God, as the servant's goodwill flows from the fear of God" [Theophylact]. Even slaves, low as is their status, should not think the influence of their example a matter of no consequence to religion: how much more those in a high position. His love in being "our Saviour" is the strongest ground for our adorning His doctrine by our lives. This is the force of "For" in Tit 2:11 .

"hath been manifested" (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.4">Tit 3:4</reference>), after having been long hidden in the loving counsels of God (<reference osisRef="Col.1.26">Col 1:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.9">2Ti 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>). The image is illustrated in <reference osisRef="Acts.27.20">Ac 27:20</reference>. The grace of God hath now been embodied in Jesus, the brightness of the Father's glory," manifested as the "Sun of righteousness," "the Word made flesh." The Gospel dispensation is hence termed "the day" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.5">1Th 5:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.8">8</reference>; there is a double "appearing," that of "grace" here, that of "glory," <reference osisRef="Titus.2.13">Tit 2:13</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rom.13.12">Ro 13:12</reference>). Hence God is called "our Saviour" (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.10">Tit 2:10</reference>). The very name Jesus means the same.<div eID="gen37979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to all--</hi>of whom he enumerated the different classes (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.2-Titus.2.9">Tit 2:2-9</reference>): even to servants; to us Gentiles, once aliens from God. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18278"/><div sID="gen37981" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18278"/><hi type="bold">12. Teaching--</hi>Greek, "disciplining us." Grace exercises discipline, and is imparted in connection with disciplining chastisements (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.32">1Co 11:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.6">He 12:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.7">7</reference>). The education which the Christian receives from "the grace" of God is a discipline often trying to flesh and blood: just as children need disciplining. The discipline which it exercises teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts, and to live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world (Greek, "age," or course of things) where such self-discipline is needed, seeing that its spirit is opposed to God (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.12">Tit 1:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">1Co 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.18">3:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.19">19</reference>): in the coming world we may gratify every desire without need of self-discipline, because all desires there will be conformable to the will of God.<div eID="gen37981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37982" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that--</hi>Greek, "in order that"; the end of the "disciplining" is "in order that ... we may live soberly," &c. This point is lost by the translation, "teaching us."<div eID="gen37982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37983" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">denying ... lusts--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Luke.9.23">Lu 9:23</reference>). The Greek aorist expresses "denying once for all." We deny "worldly lusts" when we withhold our consent from them, when we refuse the delight which they suggest, and the act to which they solicit us, nay, tear them up by the roots out of our soul and mind [ST. Bernard, Sermon 11].<div eID="gen37983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37984" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">worldly lusts--</hi>The Greek article expresses, "the lusts of the world," "all worldly lusts" [Alford], (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.16">Ga 5:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.3">Ep 2:3</reference>; 1Jo 2:15-17; 5:19). The world (cosmos) will not come to an end when this present age (aeon) or course of things shall end.<div eID="gen37984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37985" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">live soberly, righteously, and godly--</hi>the positive side of the Christian character; as "denying ... lusts" was the negative. "Soberly," that is, with self-restraint, in relation to one's self: "righteously" or justly, in relation to our neighbor; "godly" or piously, in relation to God (not merely amiably and justly, but something higher, godly, with love and reverence toward God). These three comprise our "disciplining" in faith and love, from which he passes to hope (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.13">Tit 2:13</reference>). <div eID="gen37985" type="x-p"/>
